The minister said India's fisherfolk are benefiting from wider market access and growing export opportunities, with seafood exports touching an all-time high during FY 2025-26. Highlighting the sector's rapid growth, Goyal said seafood exports have recorded a nearly 145 per cent jump since FY 2013-14. "Our fisherfolk are benefiting from expanded markets and rising exports, with seafood exports reaching an all-time high in FY 2025-26. With nearly 145 per cent jump in exports since FY 2013-14, India's Blue Economy is emerging as a powerful engine of growth," the minister said. Meanwhile, India's seafood exports touched an all-time high in both volume and value during 2025-26, underlining the sector's resilience amid uncertain global trade conditions and strengthening the country's position as a major supplier to international markets. India exported 19.72 lakh metric tonnes of seafood during the fiscal year, valued at Rs 73,890 crore ($8.46 billion), the highest ever achieved by the sector, the Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA) said on June 1. Announcing the figures, MPEDA Chairman P. Jawahar said the record performance was achieved despite multiple global challenges, including volatile demand patterns and market uncertainties. Frozen shrimp continued to dominate India's seafood export basket, accounting for more than two-thirds of total export earnings. MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY / ORDER
Notification S.O. 4031(E) under Section 6 of the Export (Quality Control and Inspection) Act, 1963

1. NOTIFICATION OF MARINE PRODUCTS EXPORT INSPECTION:
The Central Government notifies fresh, frozen, canned, and processed marine products (including aquaculture shrimp and cephalopods) for mandatory quality inspection and health certification prior to export to international destinations including the European Union and the United States.

2. THREE-TIER COMPLIANCE MECHANISM:
Exporters may operate under one of three statutory certification modes:
(a) Consignment-wise inspection by EIA officers;
(b) In-Process Quality Control (IPQC) for approved facilities;
(c) Food Safety Management System based on HACCP principles approved by the Inter-Departmental Panel (IDP).

3. ISSUANCE OF HEALTH CERTIFICATES:
Every shipment destined for the EU must be accompanied by an official Health Certificate signed by an authorized veterinarian/officer of the Export Inspection Agency, validating cold-chain maintenance at -18 degrees Celsius and absence of prohibited antibiotic residues.', 'Title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 - Temporary Increase of Official Controls on Third Country Imports

COMMISSION IMPLEMENTING REGULATION (EU) 2019/1793
on the temporary increase of official controls and emergency measures governing the entry into the Union of certain goods from certain third countries implementing Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and (EC) No 178/2002

1. REGULATORY PURPOSE & EMERGENCY BORDER SURVEILLANCE:
Pursuant to Article 47 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the European Commission establishes mandatory border frequency checks and emergency certification rules for feed and food originating from third countries where ongoing monitoring indicates persistent non-compliance with EU food safety legislation.

2. ANNEX II MANDATE FOR INDIAN SPICES:
Consignments of high-risk Indian agricultural products listed in Annex II—specifically Capsicum annuum (Chilli peppers and products), Myristica fragrans (Nutmeg), Cumin seeds, and Murraya koenigii (Curry leaves)—cannot enter EU Border Control Posts (BCPs) without mandatory pre-shipment health certification.

3. REQUIRED ACCOMPANYING DOCUMENTATION:
Every entry lot from India must be accompanied by:
- An Official Certificate issued by the competent authority of India (Export Inspection Council / Spices Board).
- An Analytical Test Report demonstrating compliance with EU Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) for Ethylene Oxide (ETO) and pesticide contamination, sampled within 30 days prior to container departure.

4. BORDER CONTROL POST (BCP) IDENTITY & PHYSICAL CHECKS:
EU customs authorities execute 100% documentary checks, 100% identity checks, and at least 20% identity/physical analytical sampling checks at BCPs. EXPORT INSPECTION COUNCIL OF INDIA (EIC)
CONSIGNMENT-WISE INSPECTION & HEALTH CERTIFICATION PROTOCOL FOR EXPORT OF SPICES TO EUROPEAN UNION

1. BACKGROUND & JOINT MANDATE WITH SPICES BOARD:
Pursuant to European Union special import conditions (Commission Implementing Regulation EU 2019/1793 as amended), export consignments of high-risk Indian spices—specifically Capsicum annuum (Chilli and Chilli products), Myristica fragrans (Nutmeg), and Murraya koenigii (Curry leaves)—require mandatory health certification issued by EIC/EIAs before export from India.

2. SAMPLING PROTOCOL FOR SPICE CONSIGNMENTS:
For every planned export lot, authorized EIA inspection officers must draw representative samples strictly following ISO 948 / EU sampling regulations. Samples are divided into three sealed counter-parts: one for official laboratory testing, one for exporter reference, and one retained at EIA headquarters.

3. ANALYTICAL TESTING MANDATE:
Official testing is conducted at EIA laboratories or Spices Board Quality Evaluation Laboratories (QEL) verifying strict adherence to EU Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs):
- Aflatoxin B1 (maximum 5.0 mcg/kg) and Total Aflatoxins (maximum 10.0 mcg/kg) in Chilli and Nutmeg.
- Ethylene Oxide (ETO) and 2-Chloroethanol (sum expressed as ETO below LOQ 0.05 mg/kg).
- Multi-residue pesticide screens in Curry leaves.

4. HEALTH CERTIFICATE ENDORSEMENT:
Consignments clearing analytical verification receive the statutory EIC Official Certificate signed by designated EIA inspection officers, enabling expedited green-lane entry at EU Border Control Posts.']

Opportunities and risks
Lydia Afriyie-Kraft

Centre for Development and Environment, University of Bern, Mittelstrasse 43, 3012 Bern, Switzerland

ABSTRACT
The European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) introduces strict due diligence obligations, requiring EU 
operators to trace the origin of commodities and verify that they are deforestation-free. While existing research 
has largely focused on the design of the regulation and the challenges of its enforcement, little attention has been 
paid to the role of EUDR compliance data as both a cost factor and a potential asset. This paper analyses the costs 
of EUDR compliance data, paying particular attention to the distributional effects among market actors. It also 
explores the opportunities for monetising such data and the implications for producer privacy and data pro -
tection. Our findings suggest that compliance costs may not be evenly distributed across the supply chain, with 
producers in exporting countries being particularly vulnerable. This could create unintended market distortions, 
including price shifts and the supplanting of EUDR-relevant commodities by illicit alternatives. Notably, the 
monetisation of EUDR compliance data could offer producer countries new revenue streams. However, many 
EUDR-relevant commodities originate from countries with weak data protection frameworks, raising concerns 
about the potential misuse of producers' data. While data monetisation could help offset EUDR compliance costs, 
it must be accompanied by robust data protection laws. We recommend harmonising, strengthening and 
enforcing data protection laws in producer countries to ensure that the benefits of EUDR compliance are not 
achieved at the expense of the most vulnerable. Addressing these issues is critical to aligning the EUDR with 
broader objectives of sustainability, fairness and inclusive global value chains.
1. Introduction
Data and data processing with artificial intelligence are increasingly 
seen as tools to support sustainability transitions ( Aaronson and Leb -
lond, 2018 ; Galaz et al., 2021 ; Hassani et al., 2021 ; Vance et al., 2024 ). 
Several novel environmental Regulations enacted by the European 
Union (EU) rely on the provision of large amounts of data for compliance 
reporting, notably the EU Regulation on Deforestation-Free Products 
(EUDR), the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, the EU 
Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive and the EU taxonomy. 
Together, these environmental Regulations support the implementation 
of the European Green Deal to transform the EU into a more resource- 
efficient and competitive economy ( EUR-Lex, 2022 ).
These Regulations also aim to help businesses, investors and con -
sumers at the EU level to identify environmentally sustainable activities 
and consumption patterns. They require economic operators to collect 
data, process it and communicate comprehensive proof of compliance. 
Collecting and processing the required data is a costly administrative 
burden ( Hoos et al., 2025 ). Concerns about the added costs of collecting 
and processing the required information along complex supply chains 
have been raised, particularly in the context of the EUDR ( Sevilla et al., 
2025 ; Urugo et al., 2025 ; Zabel et al., 2025 ).
However, beyond the overall economic burden of data collection, 
little thought has been given to the distributional effects of compliance 
costs across supply chain actors and whether there could be opportu -
nities for monetising the aggregated data to cover the cost. A further key 
aspect that has not been sufficiently addressed in the context of inter -
national data-driven sustainability policies is data protection. This paper 
takes an economic and policy perspective to analyse how the EUDR 
compliance data requirements could potentially distort markets. It 
further explores opportunities and risks of monetising compliance data 
to offset the costs of collecting data for compliance.
The EUDR aims to prevent deforestation-related and illegally pro -
duced commodities from entering the EU market ( Regulation EU 2023/ 
1115 ). Commodities covered by the EUDR include cocoa, coffee, timber, 
rubber, palm oil, soy and cattle. To achieve the regulation's goals, Article

4 mandates operators (importers) to exercise due diligence before 
placing any relevant products on the EU market. As outlined in Articles 
8, 9 and 10 of the EUDR, due diligence includes collecting and assessing 
large amounts of data, e. g. geolocation data and documents proving 
legal production. This data must be collected at the beginning of each 
supply chain, processed by various actors and stored by EU operators for 
at least five years. Producers that do not pass on the relevant information 
to importers will lose access to the EU market ( Susilawati and Kanowski, 
2022 ).
Recent work and the Strategic Framework for International Coop -
eration Engagement of the European Commission characterise the 
EUDR's environmental and social aims. Accordingly, the EUDR is said to 
reduce commodity-driven deforestation, forest degradation, associated 
biodiversity and climate impacts and promote sustainable practices 
( Beltrame de Moura, 2025 ; European Commission, 2024 ; Srivastava and 
Banerjee, 2025 ). Furthermore, the EU Commission envisions the EUDR 
as a tool to fulfil the SDG commitment and the Paris Agreement. The 
Regulation is also seen as an opportunity to enhance responsible trade 
and boost opportunities for inclusion and equity among actors around 
the globe ( Beltrame de Moura, 2025 ; European Commission, 2024 ; 
Linden et al., 2025 ).
Although the Regulation is well intended, its normative goals do not 
fully reflect the complex socio-economic realities of producer countries. 
Instead, they are influenced by a combination of the convictions and 
interests of NGOs, EU institutions and multinational businesses, while 
initially ignoring the perspectives of governments and smallholders in 
producer countries ( Berning and Sotirov, 2024 ; van Noordwijk et al., 
2025 ). It also fails to clarify who should pay for data collection and how 
the costs should be shared between the relevant parties ( Muradian et al., 
2025 ). We argue that in the absence of initiatives addressing imple -
mentation barriers ( Azevedo-Ramos and Lima, 2024 ), the EUDR could 
be at risk of issues such as supplier substitution and market shifts, as was 
observed with its predecessor, the EU Timber Regulation (EUTR) 
( European Commission, 2023 ; K ¨othke et al., 2023 ; K ¨othke, 2020 ; Schulz 
et al., 2026 ). This in turn may jeopardise rather than promote sustain -
ability goals ( Beltrame de Moura, 2025 ).
Besides environmental and social aims, other important normative 
goals of the Regulation include traceability and transparency. A sub -
stantial body of literature has examined the benefits of transparent 
supply chains ( Gardner et al., 2019 ; Schilling-Vacaflor and Gustafsson, 
2024 ), particularly the EUDR's potential contribution to sustainable 
forest management, environmental governance and deforestation free 
and legal commodity supply chains. These include the reduction of 
global deforestation and forest degradation, the protection of biodiver -
sity, the mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as well as the promotion 
of legality and traceability of supply chains ( Cosimo et al., 2024 ; Dur ´an, 
2025 ; Johnston et al., 2025 ; Muradian et al., 2025 ; Tonou ´ewa et al., 
2024 ).
Existing literature has identified traceability as the core mechanism 
for effective forest governance and sustainable forest management 
( Mensah et al., 2025 ; Muradian et al., 2025 ; Tonou ´ewa et al., 2024 ). 
Traceability systems are thus necessary for achieving the zero- 
deforestation supply chain commitments ( Fripp et al., 2023 ). They 
link products and actors to origin, enabling accountability and 
enforcement along global commodity chains ( Gardner et al., 2019 ). 
Traceability technologies promote transparent markets, efficient forest 
resource management and reputational confidence ( Lima et al., 2025 ; 
Stopfer et al., 2024 ).
Although Cosimo et al. (2024) and Muradian et al. (2025) identified 
gaps in several existing traceability systems, other studies report that 
traceability systems such as certification have reduced illegal logging, 
improved sustainable practices, forest governance, enforcement of legal 
requirements, accountability and market efficiency ( Elias, 2024 ; Men -
sah et al., 2025 ). Miniarti et al. (2018) reported that the Indonesian 
Timber Legality Verification System has increased legality and sustain -
ability compliance in supply chains in the country. In the Amazon, 
innovative traceability technologies such as isotopic analysis or big data 
are seen as promising solutions to legality verification and reducing 
illegal logging ( Lima et al., 2025 ). Certification, third party-verification 
systems and traceability through due diligence systems in Europe have 
contributed to compliance with the EUTR ( Gavrilut et al., 2016 ). Heil -
mayr and Lambin (2016) reported a reduction in deforestation when 
certification was combined with stakeholder collaboration in Chile. 
However, Muradian et al. (2025) reported that these systems have failed 
to stop deforestation.
Against this backdrop, the EU Joint Research Centre has developed 
the EU Observatory on Deforestation and Forest Degradation to support 
global forest monitoring and contribute to stopping deforestation. Spe -
cifically, the EU Observatory provides global forest data to help opera -
tors and authorities assess the risk of deforestation and degradation and 
support due diligence ( Vogt and Caudullo, 2022 ). Furthermore, multi -
lateral agencies and organisations like the International Trade Centre, 
Fraunhofer Institute for Material Flow and Logistics and the Food and 
Agriculture Organisation are developing platforms to support data 
collection for EUDR compliance ( FAO, 2024 ; Frauenhofer, 2023 ; Inter -
national Trade Center, I, 2024 ). However, these tools mainly focus on 
the deforestation aspect of the EUDR. Therefore, producers must still 
provide the legal information required, as outlined in the EUDR Guid -
ance documents ( European Commission, 2025a ). Moreover, producers 
require expertise to operate the tools, collect data and pass it on to their 
EU-based customers. Likewise, EU operators require expertise or third- 
party assistance to apply EUDR-compliant due diligence systems. All 
these come at a cost that must be borne by the supply chain actors.
Although essential to the Regulation's objectives, data requirements 
of the EUDR raise two under-examined issues. First, who pays for the 
cost of collecting data for compliance? Compliance costs for importers 
arise from setting up and applying a due diligence system, submitting 
due diligence statements and complying with public reporting and data 
retention obligations ( Rijk and Kuepper, 2024 ). In addition, producers 
face substantial costs when gathering information on legality and geo -
location ( Mabica et al., 2025 ). Second, what happens to the data 
collected for compliance?
Our study builds on these perspectives by analysing through an 
economic lens the implications of data requirements for compliance for 
producers and EU importers. It also offers insight into opportunities for 
monetising producers' data to offset costs of collecting data and to 
ensure that the Regulation supports not only environmental integrity, 
but also inclusive and sustainable trade.
2. Distribution of cost and data monetisation
How the costs are distributed can depend on supply and demand 
elasticities as well as political factors such as the actors' bargaining 
power or their capacity to strategically reposition within supply chains. 
This section focuses on the former and examines how elasticities influ -
ence the distribution of costs and explores the opportunities for data 
monetisation. The latter ranges from basic data sales to optimising 
market performance through complex data-driven services ( Ritala et al., 
2024 ). Ultimately, this analysis aims to provide insights into sustainable 
cost recovery strategies within EUDR-regulated supply chains. It is 
important to emphasise that producers are heterogeneous ( Susilawati 
et al., 2019 ; Susilawati and Kanowski, 2022 ; Zhunusova et al., 2022 ). 
Hence, compliance costs and capabilities may differ widely between 
small-scale producers, out-growers and large companies, the type of 
product and even the risk category of the country ( Directorate-General 
for Environment, 2025 ; van Noordwijk et al., 2025 ; Wolff and 
Schweinle, 2022 ). While our analysis remains at the conceptual level, 
further studies could empirically examine the actual cost implications 
and distributional effects among different actors once EUDR imple -
mentation begins.

5. Equipment & Machinery:
5.1 The equipment and fittings in slaughter hall except for chopping blocks, cutting boards and brooms, shall
be of such material and of such construction as to enable them to be kept clean. The implements shall be of metal or

5.2 No vessel, container or other equipment, the use of which is likely to cause metallic contamination
injurious to health shall be employed in the preparation, packing or storage of meat food products. (Copper or brass
vessels shall always be heavily lined. No iron or galvanised iron shall come in contact with meat food products).
6. Personnel Hygiene:
6.1 No person suffering from infectious or contagious diseases shall be allowed to work in the factory.
Arrangements shall be made to get the factory staff medically examined at such intervals as the licensing authority
deems fit, to ensure that they are free from infectious, contagious and other diseases. A record of these examinations

6.2 The staff shall be inoculated against the enteric group of diseases and a certificate thereof shall be kept for

which shall be clean. The management shall ensure that all workers are neat, clean and tidy.
(a) Animal Welfare
Animal welfare is a major concern in meat production. It is essential that animals be reared, handled,
transported, and slaughtered using humane practices. A healthy and peaceful animal is an essential requirement
for hygienic slaughter and safety of the meat product.
Careful handling of animals during loading / unloading, transportation and at slaughtering helps in improving
the quality of meat and reduction in losses in the value of the carcass/meat.

Livestock are transported en masse from the farm to the slaughterhouse, a process called "live export". Depending

stressed animals are low in water and glycogen, and their pH fails to attain acidic values.

4.5 Drainage and waste disposal
4.5.1 Food waste and other waste materials shall be removed periodically from the place where food is being
handled or cooked or manufactured to avoid building up. A refuse bin of adequate size with a proper cover
preferably one which need not be touched for opening shall be provided in the premises for collection of waste
material. This shall be emptied and washed daily with a disinfectant and dried before next use.
4.5.2 The disposal of sewage and effluents (solid, liquid and gas) shall be in conformity with requirements of
Factory / Environment Pollution Control Board. Adequate drainage, waste disposal systems and facilities shall be
provided and they shall be designed and constructed in such manner so that the risk of contaminating food or the
potable water supply is eliminated.
4.5.3 Waste storage shall be located in such manner that it does not contaminate the food process, storage
areas, the environment inside and outside the food establishment and waste shall be kept in covered containers and
shall be removed at regular intervals.
4.5.4 Periodic disposal of the refuse / waste should be made compulsory. No waste shall be kept open inside
the premise and shall be disposed of in an appropriate manner as per local rules and regulations including those for
plastics and other non environment friendly materials.
4.6 Personnel facilities and toilets
4.6.1 Personnel facilities shall include those for proper washing and drying of hands before touching food
materials including wash basins and a supply of hot and /or cold water as appropriate; separate lavatories, of
appropriate hygienic design, for males and females separately; and changing facilities for personnel and such
facilities shall be suitably located so that they do not open directly into food processing, handling or storage areas.
4.6.2 Number of toilets should be adequate depending on the number of employees (male /female) in the
establishment and they should be made aware of the cleanliness requirement while handling food.
4.6.3 Rest and refreshments rooms shall be separate from food process and service areas and these areas shall
not lead directly to food production, service and storage areas.
4.6.4 A display board mentioning do's & don'ts for the workers shall be put up inside at a prominent place in
the premise in English or in local language for everyone's understanding.
4.7 Air quality and ventilation
Ventilation systems natural and /or mechanical including air filters, exhaust fans, wherever required, shall be
designed and constructed so that air does not flow from contaminated areas to clean areas.
4.8 Lighting
Natural or artificial lighting shall be provided to the food establishment, to enable the employees/workers to
operate in a hygienic manner. Lighting fixtures must wherever appropriate, be protected to ensure that food is not
contaminated by breakages of electrical fittings.
5 FOOD OPERATIONS AND CONTROLS
5.1 Procurement of raw materials
5.1.1 No raw material or ingredient thereof shall be accepted by an establishment if it is known to contain
parasites, undesirable micro-organisms, pesticides, veterinary drugs or toxic items, decomposed or extraneous
substances, which would not be reduced to an acceptable level by normal sorting and/or processing.
5.1.2 All raw materials, food additives and ingredients, wherever applicable, shall conform to all the Regulations
and standards laid down under the Act.
5.1.3 Records of raw materials, food additives and ingredients as well as their source of procurement shall be
maintained in a register for inspection.
5.1.4 All raw materials should be checked & cleaned physically thoroughly.
5.1.5 Raw materials should be purchased in quantities that correspond to storage/ preservation capacity.
5.1.6 Packaged raw material must be checked for 'expiry date'/ 'best before'/ 'use by' date, packaging integrity
and storage conditions.

5.1.7 Receiving temperature of potentially high risk food should be at or below 5 0C
5.1.8 Receiving temperature of frozen food should be -18 0C or below.
5.2 Storage of raw materials and food
5.2.1 Food storage facilities shall be designed and constructed to enable food to be effectively protected from
contamination during storage; permit adequate maintenance and cleaning, to avoid pest access and accumulation.
5.2.2 Cold Storage facility, wherever required, shall be provided to raw, processed / packed food according to
the type and requirement.
5.2.3 Segregation shall be provided for the storage of raw, processed, rejected, recalled or returned materials
or products which will be distinguishably marked and secured. Raw materials and food shall be stored in separate
areas from printed packaging materials, stationary, hardware and cleaning materials / chemicals.
5.2.4 Raw food, particularly meat, poultry and seafood products shall be cold stored separately from the area
of work-in-progress, processed, cooked and packaged products. The conditions of storage in terms of temperature
and humidity requisite for enhancing the shelf life of the respective food materials / products shall be maintained.
5.2.5 Storage of raw materials, ingredients, work-in-progress and processed / cooked or packaged food
products shall be subject to FIFO (First in, First Out), FEFO (First Expire First Out) stock rotation system as
applicable.
5.2.6 Containers made of non-toxic materials shall be provided for storage of raw materials, work-in-progress
and finished / ready to serve products. The food materials shall be stored on racks / pallets such that they are
reasonably well above the floor level and away from the wall so as to facilitate effective cleaning and prevent
harbouring of any pests, insects or rodents.
5.3 Food Processing / Preparation, Packaging and Distribution / Service
5.3.1.Time and temperature control
5.3.1.1 The Food Business shall develop and maintain the systems to ensure that time and temperature are
controlled effectively where it is critical to the safety and suitability of food. Such control shall include time and
temperature of receiving, processing, cooking, cooling, storage, packaging, distribution and food service upto the
consumer, as applicable.
5.3.1.2 Whenever frozen food / raw materials are being used / handled / transported, proper care should be
taken so that defrosted / thawed material are not stored back after opening for future use.
5.3.1.3 If thawing is required then only required portion of the food should be thawed at a time.
5.3.1.4 Wherever cooking is done on open fire, proper outlets for smoke/steam etc. like chimney, exhaust fan
etc. shall be provided.
5.4 Food Packaging
5.4.1 Packaging materials shall provide protection for all food products to prevent contamination, damage and shall
accommodate required labelling as laid down under the FSS Act & the Regulations there under.
5.4.2 For primary packaging (i.e packaging in which the food or ingredient or additive comes in direct contact with
the packaging material), only Food grade packaging materials are to be used . For packaging materials like aluminium
plastic and tin, the standards to be followed are as mentioned under the FSS Regulations and rules framed there under.
5.4.3 Packaging materials or gases where used, shall be non-toxic and shall not pose a threat to the safety and
suitability of food under the specified conditions of storage and use.
5.5 Food Distribution / Service
5.5.1 All critical links in the supply chain need to be identified and provided for to minimize food spoilage during
transportation. Processed / packaged and / or ready-to-eat food shall be protected as per the required storage conditions
during transportation and / or service.
5.5.2 Temperatures and humidity which are necessary for sustaining food safety and quality shall be maintained.
The conveyances and /or containers shall be designed, constructed and maintained in such manner that they can
effectively maintain the requisite temperature, humidity, atmosphere and other conditions necessary to protect food"]

Representative_Docs:
['[Page 8]
around our four key contingencies, focusing on how they facilitate (or 
inhibit) identifying modern slavery by leveraging monitoring technol -
ogies through multi-actor collaboration. Collectively, the findings pro -
vide a basis for directly answering our research question.
4.1. Modern slavery posture
Modern slavery posture refers to the reason why an organization 
pursues collaboration. There are many reasons why various actors in 
supply chains do not want modern slavery to be found. For example, it 
can be highly profitable for those exploiting others. However, they could 
also be severely punished if it is located, such as reputational risk for a 
firm, or criminal liability for an individual. Motivation is thus impactful 
in determining the modern slavery posture of any given actor – a firm, 
auditing body or NGO. This is illustrated by the following quote: 
“In terms of how difficult is it to find, it is. It depends on whether 
you’re looking for it and it depends on whether you want to find it.” 
MS4
The contracts- and conditions-focused domains provide contrasting 
environments in which modern slavery is identified. We note that many 
interviewees indicated the existence of these domains, though the ter -
minology used to describe them varied. For example: 
“I think those are kind of the two camps that I’ve noticed. One kind 
tends to be used to cater to corporations’ risk-based approach and 
then the NGOs tend to come in for more continuous improvement 
approach. Or not necessarily always NGOs, they could be consul -
tancies, they could be social enterprises, but I think there’s a bit more 
potentially, a more holistic approach to looking at the root cause 
rather than a compliance-based approach.” MS7
In the contracts-focused domain, firms seek collaborations and 
secure resources predominantly to acquire compliance with standards 
and other reference points. In fact, respondents frequently referred to 
this domain as the “compliance-domain” in the interviews. Firms are 
increasingly pushed to address modern slavery through audits, certifi -
cations, and other compliance mechanisms and look for actors that can 
provide such services. We also heard many comments about audits 
focused on confirming the absence of modern slavery, in many cases as a 
mechanism to avoid trouble. To illustrate, 
“I think that the compliance-based approach is very familiar to 
companies. So, I think many of them still seek social audits as from a 
compliance-based perspective and a risk mitigation, risk minimiza -
tion perspective. But there is definitely a trend now and a lot of 
spotlight on companies that move away from trouble, some suppliers 
or regions or commodities, rather than actually working with the 
supply chain to improve it.” MS7
The contracts domain is thus characterized by actors whose primary 
interest is in confirming the absence of modern slavery in their supply 
chains, not necessarily identifying (and remediating) it. Moreover, this 
domain is dominated by firms and service providers. Although other 
actors might get involved (e.g., an NGO might assist with data collec -
tion), this involvement tends to be limited or reduced to symbolic col -
laborations. Notably, and consistent with RDT, the firms and service 
providers have significant control and discretion over the allocation of 
resources and their use. For example, the audits (and related data) have 
a commercial value, which is protected and leveraged for the benefit of 
participating actors (i.e., a certificate demonstrates absence of modern 
slavery). Actors in the contracts-focused domain are primarily con -
cerned with improvements of the audit process, such as cost-cutting or 
audit integration.
In the conditions-focused domain, actors are interested in identifying 
the presence of modern slavery (and then working to remediate it). This 
domain is dominated by NGOs, labour unions, and other actors whose 
raison d’etre is different from firms seeking compliance and 
certification. These actors also employ different mechanisms to identify 
modern slavery: there is less focus on audits and more focus on inves -
tigative work and working with local communities as the following 
quote illustrates: 
“NGOs are going to identify [modern slavery] better, but also it’s not 
just sort of putting a red dot on a map to say there is forced labour 
there. An NGO is going to do a better job of working with a local 
community and identifying what the appropriate remedy is. Because, 
in the end what’s going to prevent forced labour in a particular in -
dustry or what’s going to stop existing forced labour or what’s going 
to remedy forced labour is kind of context specific.” MS27
Recognizing the two modern slavery domains has important rami -
fications for selecting collaborating partners since each domain has 
different aims and approaches to identifying modern slavery. From a 
RDT perspective, for instance, it means that actors seek to secure 
different resources and align (or naturally drift toward) a domain that 
provides such resources and which allows the actors control over the 
allocation of resources for their intended purpose. An example might be 
a firm that seeks to legitimize practices in their supply chains (but not 
necessarily improve these practices), is likely to collaborate with actors 
that provide such service. Consequently, the selection and adaptation of 
technologies also serves as a tool to leverage the legitimization of supply 
chain practices. For example, worker voice technologies (WVT) can be 
used to actively conceal labour issues by careful selection of participants 
or through persecution of whistle blowers. Hotlines can be similarly 
used to monitor the workforce and identify workers the company may 
view as problematic. Conversely, technologies supporting more genuine 
motivations can have the opposite effect.
The adoption of specific monitoring technologies is driven by the 
objectives of the collaboration. For example, an organization may seek 
improvements to its data collection process to achieve greater audit 
efficiency – a typical approach for actors operating in the contracts 
focused domain. Actors involved in audits can benefit from the digita -
lization of the audit process enabled by various technologies (e.g., data 
collection platforms; phone-based apps, etc.). As the following quote 
illustrates, this can enhance audit efficiency: 
“I think technology in the audit process, I mean certainly one thing 
that’s helped is for the auditors to be able to answer the questions. On 
their audit protocol for them to be able to go through and answer 
those questions you know kind of in real time. And you know just 
save them time and energy and also as soon as you’re writing a piece 
of paper and transferring it. […] The fact that the reports get auto -
matically uploaded to [audit platform X] or [audit platform Y] or 
whomever I think that’s also really helpful …” MS9
4.2. Collaboration scope
We found two principal modes of collaborations: micro-level collab -
orations enable identifying modern slavery at a facility level, whilst 
macro-level collaborations enable the same at a regional or national level. 
In both domains, collaborations to secure resources and capabilities 
emerge at these two levels. In the contracts-focused domain, collabo -
rations emerge to enhance the efficiency of compliance mechanisms, 
such as audits. In the conditions-focused domain, the focus was on 
mobilizing communities to identify modern slavery (see Table 5 ). Cross 
boundary collaboration is also possible, as we explore in Section 4.3 .
Collaborations engaged in by each actor depends on the modern 
slavery posture. For example, audits performed at individual facilities 
could be used for multiple purposes – an activity typical for the 
contracts-focused domain. This is a focus of so-called audit platforms – 
data collection and exchange mechanisms, which are developed to 
enable an exchange of insights gained through an audit at one facility to 
inform further insights for various supply chain actors, who use the same 
facility. If actors collaborate across the micro- and macro-levels, audit

results and other data can be shared to explicitly serve the interests of 
multiple actors. This means that audit requirements can reflect the needs 
of multiple actors; an integrated audit can therefore cover areas that 
would normally require multiple audits, thus contributing to audit 
optimization. The connection between the modern slavery posture, se -
lection of a collaborator, and choice of monitoring technology is high -
lighted by the following quote: 
“So, where we’ve partnered with people, like [software platform], 
….. They had a very similar mindset to us. We set up us originally 
because we recognized that there were so many different platforms, 
so many different certifications, everything like that. And then sup -
pliers are just exhausted because they’re having to answer every -
thing separately, I mean that’s a full-time job for a few people.” MS12
The collaborations in the conditions-focused domain tend to involve 
multiple actors who collaborate for a ‘greater good’. These collabora -
tions, which underscore mutual dependencies in building capacity and 
social capital in service of the larger goal of identifying modern slavery, 
can also occur at both the micro- and macro-levels. At a micro-level, 
these collaborations aim to interlink local and other actors. To provide 
one example that was raised serveral times in our interviews, an NGO 
may work with local communities to gain on-the-ground insights on the 
labour conditions of workers. At a macro-level, the actors collaborate to 
identify modern slavery in a particular location, but also work together 
to collect insights across regions and identify hotspots of modern 
slavery. If hotspots are identified in a particular area, the insights can be 
used for local actors to follow-up and investigate. Importantly, these 
insights are rarely developed by any one actor on their own, further 
underscoring mutual dependencies. 
“The technology has enabled not only to facilitate expedited opera -
tion of the hotline, but also [to] connect the resources through these 
different platforms of Salesforce and volunteers and do this heat 
map, where the situation and geospatial location, etc., […] We 
analyze all these different sorts of information that we’re gathering 
from the interaction with survivors of trafficking to sort of identify 
certain trends, when [the] same addresses and information about 
trafficking comes [up] over and over so, then we can eventually 
develop customized packages for law enforcement about information 
about traffickers, never about victims because [of] confidentiality.” 
MS11
The collaborations across micro- and macro-levels enable exchange 
of insights and data for mutual benefit. Technology can enable the ex -
change of insights (such as data or results of analytics). Whilst the free 
flow of data is essential for collaborations, the flow of data is often 
difficult to achieve. To start with, standardization of data collection is 
critical, and this will be based on the need to coordinate and collaborate 
with many actors. Many respondents explained that the lack of data 
format standards and standardized data collection processes hampered 
effective data exchange between actors: 
“So one of the kind of main criticisms of the social audit world is lack 
of standardization in the questions that are being asked and the data 
that’s being collected. […] It’s really, really hard then to kind of 
amalgamate that data together and make comparisons if everybody’s 
looking at different things at different times …” MS6
In part, the exchange of data is influenced by a willingness of indi -
vidual actors to collaborate. This willingness is often grounded in the 
trust, or lack thereof, between potential collaborators. For example, 
complicated agreements over who owns the data may prevent collabo -
ration. An illustration is whether service providers of worker voice 
technologies (WVT) own the collected data. Depending on any partic -
ular agreement, they may collaborate on projects where they are in 
control of the data or outsource their technology to actors who own (yet 
not further share) the data.
Other monitoring technological solutions may have fewer pro -
prietary restrictions. For example, satellites are increasingly being used 
to monitor large geographic areas (e.g., forests, shrimp farms, food 
processing facilities). While not necessarily definitive, this type of data 
can highlight potential risks requiring further investigation, mindful of 
the cost of acquiring this data. The benefit of using it is that local actors 
could be alerted to verify any concerns, as the following explains: 
“We have a couple of projects where we’re looking at using satellite 
imagery of monitoring forests. […] There’s some kind of the satellite 
spots deforestation, a quick survey goes out to a group of, you know, 
at local community members asking them, hey, what’s going on? Can 
you find out? That kind of triangulation of data I think is kind of the 
future of integrating these technologies together because if we’re all 
collecting information in silos and not sharing, we’re not really 
leveraging.” MS7
Technology can also enable firms to push data collection deep into 
their supply chains, including well beyond the first tier. This requires 
technological interoperability, but it also requires trust throughout the 
chain on how the data will be collected and used, particularly given the 
sensitivities around an issue like modern slavery. Financial and infor -
mational resources must thus be supported by trust, legitimacy, and an 
understanding of local contexts. In cases where trust-building is at an 
early stage, monitoring technology can enable anonymous reporting, 
which could compromise identification of issues at the micro-level, but 
might enable improved analytics at the macro-level – as illustrated by 
the following quote: 
“So it’s the lower tiers where most of the risk is because the funding 
and the work isn’t getting down that far. But if I was a tier one 
supplier and I don’t want to be cut out with the supply chain, how do 
I share that information with my brands at all? I think that allowing 
anonymous reporting is important so that you can at least find the 
risks and then figure out where to go for those suppliers that are 
particularly edgy about working with the suppliers to capacity 
building […] But then letting the suppliers have hold of that data, 
you know in our system if it’s multi tier. The tier one supplier gets to 
crunch all of the data and run analytics on their suppliers, and it 
trickles down the chain. They can look at what’s going on with the

firms can simultaneously adopt symbolic and substantive practices to 
address non-financial issues such as quality or sustainability issues 
( Prajogo et al., 2021 ), they can also simultaneously adopt approaches 
that fall within and bridge the contracts- or conditions-focused domains. 
Little is currently understood, however, about how the two domains 
co-exist and how activities within each domain interact. This is impor -
tant given the need to understand how different collaborations can 
leverage different monitoring technologies within and across the two 
domains to identify modern slavery.
2.2. Collaboration to identify modern slavery
Collaboration occurs when “two or more independent companies 
work jointly to plan and execute supply chain operations with greater 
success than when acting in isolation” ( Simatupang and Sridharan, 
2002 ). Given such a broad definition, it is clear that multiple forms of 
collaborations exist in global supply chains, from strategic alliances to 
more arms-length collaborations ( Hayes et al., 2005 ). Moreover, col -
laborations are driven by context: there is no single best way or blue -
print on how different actors collaborate. Fundamentally, collaborations 
are pursued to increase success of involved actors in achieving their 
objectives. These could include, for example, instrumental objectives 
focused on identifying modern slavery to prevent firm reputational 
damage. Collaboration can also be altruistic in nature, recognizing the 
moral obligation to remedy severe worker exploitation ( Pannekoek 
et al., 2023 ).
The main types of supply chain collaboration strategies are hori -
zontal and vertical integration ( Barratt, 2004 ). Horizontal collaboration 
occurs when two or more competing or unrelated firms (at the same 
level of the supply chain) cooperate to share resources, such as 
manufacturing capacity. Horizontal collaboration has been examined in 
response to modern slavery and requires relational capital and effective 
governance mechanisms to succeed ( Benstead et al., 2018 ). Vertical 
collaboration occurs at different levels of the supply chain – with cus -
tomers, internally (across functions), service providers, and with sup -
pliers ( Barratt, 2004 ). Collaborations between different producers, 
distributors and other actors enables a more contextualized approach in 
supply chains ( Caputo and Mininno, 1996 ), arguably providing more 
scope to strengthen labour standards and conditions ( LeBaron, 2021 ).
Collaboration is an area of increasing focus in sustainable supply 
chain research including the need for cross disciplinary scholarship 
( Kach et al., 2025 ), but social concerns, such as extreme labour condi -
tions, have rarely been studied in this context ( Geng et al., 2017 ). Much 
of the limited research that exists focuses on relationships between 
buyers and suppliers, suppliers for a common buyer ( Touboulic and 
Walker, 2015 ), or buyers with common suppliers ( Nidumolu et al., 
2014 ). Collaborative practices to identify modern slavery are critical, as 
they do not just impact source firms but can enhance the capabilities of 
other actors to reduce modern slavery risks, such as suppliers ( Emberson 
et al., 2022 ). Suppliers may adapt their vertical and horizontal re -
lationships to reduce the risk of modern slavery through strategies such 
as horizontal systemization, vertical systemization, horizontal trans -
formation, and vertical differentiation ( Emberson et al., 2022 ). The 
implication is that collaboration recognizes and promotes agency among 
the different actors to enact a range of complementary and mutually 
beneficial outcomes for all.
Collaborations beyond supplier and buyer relationships, particularly 
in a modern slavery context, can involve direct interventions, awareness 
campaigns, or government advocacy for policy changes, among others. 
Collaboration to combat modern slavery typically starts by building 
coalitions where firms, NGOs, and government agencies mobilize 
around a common goal ( Gutierrez-Huerter et al., 2023 ). Many initiatives 
focus on raising awareness to help prevent exploitation ( Bales, 2012 ), or 
on training and capacity building. Corporations, NGOs, and govern -
ments often work together to train law enforcement, immigration offi -
cials, and social service providers on human trafficking issues ( Raineri 
and Strazzari, 2022 ). Collaboration on supplier audits is another form of 
collaboration. Based on a study of 35 brands, an NGO, and a trade body, 
Benstead et al. (2018) investigated how horizontal collaboration can 
enable responses to modern slavery legislation in the textiles and fashion 
industry. Fransen and LeBaron (2019) examined the role of the “Big 
Four” audit firms in services connected to transnational labor gover -
nance. Drawing on a case study linked to modern slavery, they found 
that auditing firms “engage in a variety of informal and covert influ -
encing practices”, such as in promoting incremental improvements to 
soft-law labor governance and serving as civil society’s independent 
watchdog ( Fransen and LeBaron, 2019 , p. 260). Gold et al. (2015) also 
highlighted the need for multi-actor approaches to address modern 
slavery.
2.3. Using technology to identify modern slavery in supply chains
Technology can be broadly defined as “the practical application of 
knowledge especially in a particular area” or “a manner of accom -
plishing a task especially using technical processes, methods, or 
knowledge”, among many other possible formulations.

In this paper, 
we focus specifically on monitoring technologies. Monitoring technol -
ogies can be classified as a form of “indirect” technologies. Unlike direct 
technologies (i.e., technologies that enable transformation of inputs into 
outputs, such as trucks, flexible manufacturing systems or material 
processing technologies), indirect technologies focus on controlling and 
coordinating direct processes. Technology has been used to support 
broader social compliance audits, with a recent Gartner report providing 
a set of categories to structure thinking about its potential application 
( Cossio and McNeill, 2021 ).
Table 1 groups monitoring technologies into three main categories: 
technologies enabling data collection, data exchange, and data ana -
lytics. First, monitoring technologies can be used for data collection, 
either on-site or in a specific geographic area. For example, landlines 
and video cameras are frequently used at the facility-level. Data 
collection can be enabled by the use of satellite imaging in a broader 
geographic area ( Reid and Castka, 2023 ). Second, monitoring technol -
ogies can be used for data exchange. Technologies can be used to ensure 
interoperability between actors, which is important for any form of 
collaboration ( Herding and Fischer, 2015 ). At a facility, for example, 
smart phones might be used by auditors to upload data in shareable 
formats to apps connected to broader audit platforms ( Castka and 
Searcy, 2023 ). Blockchain can then provide an unalterable ledger to 
provide confidence on product provenance throughout a supply chain. 
Third, monitoring technologies can be used to help draw conclusions 
about the data collected through data analytics. For example, algorthims 
could be developed to predict modern slavery hotspots. Research on the 
specific use of technologies to identify modern slavery has started to 
emerge, including the use of technology to improve product traceability 
( McGrath et al., 2021 ), using blockchain ( Christ and Helliar, 2021 ), 
applying worker voice technologies ( Berg et al., 2020 ; Taylor and Shih, 
2019 ), and applying satellite imaging ( Kougkoulos et al., 2021 ). More 
broadly, institutional pressures have been shown to encourage digital 
technology adoption by firms seeking to alleviate modern slavery risks 
( Jiang et al., 2023 ).
Technology is being increasingly incorporated to facilitate collabo -
rations between different actors and optimize the use and allocation of 
resources ( Castka and Searcy, 2023 ). These collaborations are usually

Previous studies have demonstrated that actors tend to focus on 
developing collaborations that assist them in advancing their strategic 
goals ( Shiu et al., 2023 ); for example by developing dyadic relationships 
with individual actors such as certifiers ( Castka et al., 2015 ). Organi -
zations operating in such institutional environments thus primarily seek 
to maintain their autonomy ( Drees and Heugens, 2013 ). In the context of 
modern slavery, the autonomy is, in part, preserved by membership in a 
particular institutional domain (i.e., contracts-focused domain). Our 
study has extended understanding of the contracts-focused and 
conditions-focused domains (i.e. Simpson et al., 2021 ), establishing the 
conditions under which actors are more likely to leverage monitoring 
technologies and develop mutual dependencies commensurate with 
relevant strategic goals. We also identified micro- and macro-levels of 
collaboration as well as collaborations within and between the domains 
(see Table 5 ).
The common perspective of RDT is to focus on the performance of the 
dependent (focal) organization, as earlier reviews and meta-analyses 
have widely observed ( Drees and Heugens, 2013 ; Hillman et al., 2009 ; 
Ozturk, 2021 ). Our study of collaboration and technology extends the 
focus of RDT to a multi-actor context, while providing theoretical con -
tributions to the mutual dependence perspective of RDT. RDT’s mutual 
dependence perspective has often been used in contexts where “firm 
autonomy (fear of dependency) is no longer the key goal of firms in 
acquiring external resources” ( Shiu et al., 2023 ). Meta-organizations or 
other forms of decentralized multi-actor networks tend to focus on 
persuasion to commit others to exchange resources rather than using 
power ( Shiu et al., 2023 ). Few actors alone are unlikely to possess all of 
the resources needed to identify modern slavery, demonstrating the 
need to acquire important resources held by others ( Pfeffer and Salancik, 
1978 ).
5.3. Practical implications
This study provides implications for a range of actor groups such as 
managers at firms, as well as for auditors, other service providers (i.e., 
organizations providing audit platforms), NGOs, and policymakers. For 
example, managers should seek applications of context-appropriate 
technology to identify modern slavery throughout their supply chains, 
noting that success will be contingent on obtaining resources held by a 
wide range of actors. This will require creating connections and transi -
tions across the micro- and macro-levels of collaboration. Moreover, 
collaborations supporting (and supported by) technology could help 
reduce the ‘psychological distance’ of modern slavery. For example, 
psychological distance can be reduced with access to timely, high ve -
racity information that “help bring events of persons perceptually 
‘closer’ to a decision-maker” ( Simpson et al., 2021 ). Worker voice 
technologies, for instance, can enable real-time data on labor conditions 
that help bring the experiences of workers that are typically far removed 
spatially and socially from managers, policymakers, or customers.
Beyond managers, there are many related implications for auditors 
and other service providers. While using monitoring technology is not 
about replacing human auditors, there are many ways it can impact how 
auditors perform their jobs. Auditor training, for example, must reflect 
the greater range of potential sources of evidence provided through 
technological applications ( Castka and Searcy, 2023 ). Moreover, the 
boundary spanning activities across the conditions- and 
contracts-focused domains enabled by collaboration, technology, and 
other resources could provide a key differentiator in the services offered 
by different auditors ( Cossio and McNeill, 2021 ).
There are also several related implications for other actors, including 
governments and NGOs. Governments, for example, should continue to 
enact legislation focused on modern slavery in supply chains, while 
being mindful that legislation alone will not identify it. Governments 
can take additional action, such as establishing trusted hotlines and 
supporting technological investments (such as through tax incentives) 
intended to identify modern slavery. Different NGOs will clearly have 
different areas of focus and hold different resources, but examples could 
include focusing on enabling local access to communities, standardizing 
data collection protocols, providing trusted platforms for data exchange, 
and developing hotspot identification capabilities. Critically, all actors 
must recognize the challenges of identifying modern slavery working on 
their own, and that this goal is best achieved by explicitly recognizing 
mutual dependencies and actively working with others to build 
collaborations.
5.4. Limitations and future research
Building on RDT, this research illuminated the interdependencies 
between actors and resources through original empirical evidence 
gathered in a modern slavery context. However, our study also had 
limitations, which provides insight into several potential areas for future 
research.
Our study used experts from multiple settings and the results should 
be seen as an aggregated framework of the shared experiences of these 
actors. Our results thus describe the circumstances under which multi- 
actor collaborations typically leverage monitoring technologies to ach -
ieve their strategic goals. The conceptual framework is explicitly pre -
sented as a building block for future work. Additionally, we did not 
attempt to identify any ‘weight’ that should be allocated against each of 
the four key contingencies we identified. Further research on the relative 
importance of different contingencies in different contexts (e.g., in terms 
of sector/region/types of supply chains/types of technologies) would be 
valuable. Locational differences, for example, are an important dimen -
sion that shape resource dependencies in unique ways including, for 
example, rates of corruption, historical or political ties, and the level of 
trade dependence between countries ( Jiang, H. et al., 2023 ). This means 
some variance in both the nature and effectiveness of collaboration 
across modern slavery contexts is likely given different country-specific 
dependencies. Research that explores such nuances will further our 
understanding of this important area.
Our study focused on identifying modern slavery. This, however, is 
only the start of efforts to address modern slavery in supply chains. 
Future research should focus on how modern slavery can be reduced and 
eliminated following its identification. The role of collaboration in 
facilitating the remediation of modern slavery is underexplored. While 
eliminating modern slavery in practice will likely require many key 
actors working together ( McLaren et al., 2024 ), further underlining the 
applicability of RDT’s mutual dependency perspective, it is also likely to 
require a strong understanding of power imbalance in the supply chain. 
Our study did not address the power imbalance perspective of RDT, but 
it could be an additional approach for considering actions to eliminate 
modern slavery. In particular, future studies can explore the circum -
stances under which actors are coerced into particular domain mem -
bership and whether such coercive mechanisms would change the 
dynamics of multi-actor collaboration, i.e., in general or specifically in 
terms of the choice of technologies adopted.
Finally, case studies on real-world applications of monitoring tech -
nologies in a modern slavery context are needed. This could include on- 
the-ground investigations of the benefits and challenges of using tech -
nology in different modern slavery settings. This would also provide 
further opportunity to study the contingencies in leveraging monitoring 
technologies through multi-actor collaboration, as well as an opportu -
nity to study how collaborations evolve over time.
6. Conclusion
One of the reasons modern slavery persists is that it can be very 
difficult to identify in practice. Modern slavery is often embedded deep 
in supply chains far from public scrutiny. This creates a “psychological 
distance” between consumers, people experiencing modern slavery, and 
supply chain managers. Given its illegality in most jurisdictions, the
